sections.executive_summary:
### Opportunity snapshot
In California, a business that sends caregivers into clients' homes to help with bathing, dressing, toileting, transfers, meals, errands, medication reminders and companionship must hold a **Home Care Organization (HCO) license** from the California Department of Social Services (CDSS) Home Care Services Branch, and every caregiver must be a **registered home care aide** on the state registry [S1][S8][S6]. The license costs **$5,603 for two years**, paid with the application [S2], and requires $1M/$3M liability insurance, workers' compensation and a $10,000 employee dishonesty bond before CDSS will issue it [S4].

The market is large and still growing. California had **2,247 licensed HCOs and 210 pending applications** in May 2025, with 433 first licensed in 2024 alone [S23]. The state's 65+ population is projected to grow from 5.7 million (2020) to just over 9 million by 2040 [S44].

### How the money really flows
Most home care in California is publicly funded through **In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS)** — 930,755 recipients in August 2026 [S21] — but **IHSS does not pay agencies**. The recipient hires an individual provider (often a family member) and the state payroll pays that person; only San Francisco uses a contract-mode agency, for about 1,100 people [S22]. IHSS is a competitor for caregivers, not a payer: it pays $20.40/hour in San Diego County and $19.64 in Los Angeles County [S21].

That leaves two real revenue sources for a new HCO: **private pay** (CareScout's 2025 California median is **$40/hour** [S24]) and **Medi-Cal managed care plans** that contract for the CalAIM Community Support **Personal Care and Homemaker Services (PCHS)** — supplementing IHSS hours, covering people waiting for IHSS, or preventing short nursing-home stays [S17]. Plans negotiate PCHS rates privately; DHCS's non-binding benchmark is $29–$38/hour with a $33 midpoint [S19].

### Bottom line
At the $40 private-pay median, an HCO paying caregivers the IHSS-competitive $20.40 wage keeps about **$977 per client per month** after caregiver pay, payroll costs and per-client expenses. A private-pay agency with 40 clients nets about **+$9,100/month** (7.9%) at 90% census, a 75-client agency about **+$27,400/month**, and a 70/30 private/PCHS mix of 60 clients about **+$15,400**. A PCHS-only agency loses money at the $33 midpoint and needs about **$34.67/hour** to break even. Profit depends most on hours sold per client and on the spread between your price and the caregiver wage — see Section 8.

### Who is served and what an HCO does
The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act defines **home care services** as non-medical services provided by a registered home care aide to a client who, because of age or disability, cannot do them alone, so the client can stay at home. They include bathing, dressing, feeding, exercising, hygiene and grooming, transferring, ambulating, positioning, toileting, help with self-administered medication, household chores, meals, laundry, errands, transportation, help with phone and mail, and companionship [S8]. An **HCO** is a licensed individual or entity that arranges these services through **affiliated home care aides** it employs; an **independent home care aide** works directly for a client and is not employed by an HCO [S8].

### What an HCO may not do
HCO aides provide non-medical care only. Skilled nursing, therapy and medications requiring a licensed professional belong to licensed home health agencies, hospices or health facilities, which are not HCOs [S8][S9].

### Who does not need an HCO license
HSC §1796.17 lists entities that are not HCOs, including licensed home health agencies and hospices, IHSS providers, employment agencies that refer independent aides, and **regional center/DDS-vendored organizations** when DDS funds the services and more than 50% of the organization's home care recipients have developmental disabilities [S9]. CDSS and DHCS have also determined that Medi-Cal **Personal Care Agencies** serving the HCBA Waiver are exempt [S16]. A general private-pay or managed-care home care business needs the HCO license.

### Regulatory framework
- **Statute:** HSC §1796.10 et seq. (13 articles covering the registry, aide registration, HCO licensure, operating requirements, fees, inspections and enforcement) [S13].
- **Licensure:** HSC §1796.37 (requirements, two-year renewal) [S4]; fees under §1796.49 [S10]; denial and revocation under §1796.38 [S12].
- **Operations:** §1796.42 (posting, insurance, bond, abuse reporting) [S5]; §1796.43 (registry, background, TB, aide separation notice) [S6]; §1796.44 (training) [S14]; §1796.45 (TB) [S7].
- **Oversight:** random, unannounced inspections and complaint investigations (§1796.52) [S11].
- **Mandated reporting:** elder and dependent adult abuse under WIC §15630 [S45][S5].
sections.licensing_pathway:
### Step-by-step
1. **Form the business.** California LLC: Articles of Organization (LLC-1) $70 and Statement of Information (LLC-12) $20 [S42]. Get an EIN [S46] and register with EDD as an employer [S33].
2. **Buy the required coverage first.** CDSS will not license without: general and professional liability of at least **$1,000,000 per occurrence / $3,000,000 aggregate**; **workers' compensation** covering affiliated aides (certificate with policy number, dates, carrier name and address); and an **employee dishonesty bond, including third-party coverage, of at least $10,000** on form HCS 402 with the State of California as beneficiary [S4][S3].
3. **Prepare Section A forms** [S1][S3]: HCS 200 (application), HCS 215 (licensee applicant information), HCS 308 (designation of responsibility — at least one person, and **a licensee cannot designate him- or herself**), HCS 309 (partnership/corporation/LLC), HCS 402 (bond), LIC 508 (criminal record statement for each applicant) and HCS 9165 (one per board member, if any).
4. **Prepare Section B documents** [S1][S3]: articles of organization or partnership agreement, job descriptions for each position, personnel policies (employment conditional on fingerprint clearance, criminal-conviction statement, TB clearance and registry listing), a **training plan** (5 hours entry-level and 5 hours annual, trainers, objectives, sample training log), the HCO program description, and insurance certificates.
5. **Mail one complete packet with the fee** — **$5,603** (2-year license), check or money order to CDSS — to: CDSS Home Care Services Branch, 744 P Street, M.S. 9-14-90, Sacramento, CA 95814 [S1][S2]. The fee is non-refundable and incomplete packets are returned in full [S3].
6. **Receipt notice.** CDSS sends your HCO number and instructions for **fingerprinting (Live Scan)** and the **online orientation** [S1]. The licensee must pass a background examination and complete the CDSS orientation before licensure [S4].
7. **License issued.** CDSS publishes no processing time; plan for several months and respond quickly to any request [S3].
8. **Hire and register aides before any client contact.** Each aide registers on the Home Care Aide Registry ($35; the HCO can submit through its own Guardian account) [S15], is Live Scanned and cleared [S6], has a TB exam 90 days before or within 7 days after hire with clearance before working [S7], and completes 5 hours of entry-level training [S14].
9. **Operate and renew.** Post the license and business hours [S5]; keep insurance and bond in force [S5]; notify CDSS immediately when an aide leaves [S6]; renew every two years with the fee postmarked by the expiration date (CDSS mails a fee notice at least 60 days before) [S4]. A $100 fee applies to a change of location and $200 to a change in corporation [S2].

### Fees at a glance
| Item | Amount | When paid |
|---|---|---|
| HCO license (2 years) | $5,603 | With the application; again at each renewal [S2][S10] |
| Home care aide registration | $35 per aide (2 years) | At registration and renewal [S15] |
| Change of location / corporation | $100 / $200 | When filed [S2] |
| LLC formation | $90 | At formation [S42] |
| Medi-Cal provider application (only if a plan requires PAVE enrollment) | $750 (CY2026) | With the enrollment application [S20] |
sections.reimbursement:
### 1. Private pay (main revenue for most HCOs)
Families pay by the hour. CareScout's 2025 survey puts the California median for a non-medical caregiver at **$40/hour**; homemaker services at 44 hours a week cost $91,520 a year [S24]. This is a statewide median; coastal metros may price higher. Long-term care insurance and Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits sometimes reimburse private-pay clients, but their terms were not verified for this report.

### 2. Medi-Cal managed care — CalAIM Community Supports
Medi-Cal managed care plans may offer **Personal Care and Homemaker Services (PCHS)** as a Community Support. PCHS covers help with ADLs and IADLs for members at risk of hospitalization or nursing-facility placement, members with functional deficits and no adequate support, and IHSS-approved members — during the IHSS application process, on top of approved IHSS hours, or (for people not eligible for IHSS) to prevent a short nursing-facility stay of up to 60 days [S17]. **IHSS must remain the primary source of support**; PCHS cannot replace an IHSS referral, and HCBA Waiver members who get Waiver Personal Care Services are not eligible [S17]. Allowable providers listed by DHCS include personal care agencies and home health agencies (non-exhaustive) [S17].

**Rates:** there is no state fee schedule. Each plan negotiates. DHCS's **non-binding** Community Supports Pricing Resource gives an hourly agency-model range of **$29 / $33 / $38** (low / midpoint / high) for codes S5130 and T1019, and the same range for Respite (H0045, S5151, S9125) [S19]. The benchmark assumes a **$15/hour** caregiver wage, one supervisor per 10 workers and 30 miles a day of travel [S19] — below today's $16.90 state minimum [S29]. DHCS says the resource is being updated [S18]. Treat the $33 midpoint as a starting point for negotiation, not a guaranteed rate.

### 3. IHSS — why it does not pay HCOs
IHSS served **930,755 recipients** with **843,828 individual providers** in August 2026, averaging 119 authorized hours per recipient per month [S21]. The recipient and the county Public Authority are the employers of record, CDSS runs a central payroll, over 70% of providers are family members, and the agency-based **contract mode exists only in San Francisco (about 1,100 people)** [S22]. IHSS providers themselves are exempt from HCO licensure [S9]. For an HCO, IHSS matters in two ways: it sets the **wage** your caregivers can earn elsewhere ($20.40 in San Diego, $19.64 in Los Angeles, $23.00 in San Francisco [S21]), and IHSS recipients who need more hours than authorized are potential private-pay or PCHS clients.

### 4. Other public payers (not modeled)
HCBA Waiver Personal Care Services are delivered by Medi-Cal Personal Care Agencies that are exempt from HCO licensure [S16]. Regional center (DDS) vendored services are exempt when DDS funds them and over 50% of recipients have developmental disabilities [S9]. VA and regional-center rates were not retrieved (see What This Report Does Not Claim). Federal law requires electronic visit verification (EVV) for Medicaid-funded personal care [S43].
sections.demand:
### Demographics
California had about **5.7 million residents age 65+ in 2020 (14%)**, projected to reach **just over 9 million (22%) by 2040**, and the 80+ population is expected to more than double [S44].

### Public-program signal
IHSS authorized **110.8 million hours** for 930,755 recipients in August 2026 — about 119 hours per recipient per month [S21] — and is projected to serve about 875,000 people in FY2026–27 under the state budget estimate cited by CHCF [S22]. These are consumer-directed hours, not agency revenue, but they show the depth of need and the pool of people who may need hours beyond their IHSS authorization (an allowed use of PCHS [S17]).

### Supply
The CDSS facility list (May 25, 2025) shows **2,247 licensed HCOs** and **210 pending**; the largest counts are Los Angeles (594), Orange (244), San Diego (230), Santa Clara (132) and Riverside (126). New licenses rose from 152 first licensed in 2017 to 433 in 2024, while 283 closed in 2024 [S23]. Competition is real, especially in Southern California metros.

### Referral sources
Private-pay referrals typically come from hospital and skilled-nursing discharge planners, senior living communities, geriatric care managers, elder-law attorneys, Area Agencies on Aging and online search. For PCHS, referrals come from the member's managed care plan (often through care management) [S17]. Referral volumes were not verified and are not claimed.
sections.operations:
### Staffing rules
The Act sets **no staffing ratios, no administrator license and no RN requirement** for HCOs. It requires:
- A licensee who passes the background exam and CDSS orientation [S4], and at least one **designee** named on HCS 308 who acts in the licensee's absence; the licensee cannot designate him- or herself [S3].
- **Affiliated home care aides age 18+**, registered on the Home Care Aide Registry [S8][S6].
- Background clearance (Live Scan) for any staff, volunteer or employee with client contact or access to confidential client information, **before** contact [S6].
- **TB clearance**: exam 90 days before or within 7 days after hire, no work until a licensed professional documents no risk, repeat every 2 years [S7].
- **Training**: at least 5 hours entry-level before client contact (2 hours orientation, 3 hours safety including infection control and emergency procedures) and 5 hours every year (client rights and safety, ADL needs, abuse and neglect reporting, hygiene assistance, safe transport); **dementia care is added to the annual topics from January 1, 2027** [S14][S3].
- Immediate notice to CDSS when an aide is no longer employed [S6].

### Required coverage and postings
Keep $1M/$3M liability, workers' comp and the $10,000 dishonesty bond in force; post the license and business hours where clients and aides can see them; report suspected elder, dependent-adult and child abuse and keep copies of reports for CDSS review [S5][S45].

### Employment law that shapes cost
- **Wages:** the 2026 state minimum is $16.90 [S29]; many cities are higher (City of Los Angeles $18.42 and unincorporated LA County $18.47 from July 1, 2026; San Francisco $19.61; Emeryville $20.34; San Diego $17.75; West Hollywood $20.25) [S30][S31]. SB 525's health care minimum wage covers licensed home health agencies but does not list HCOs [S32].
- **Overtime:** as third-party employers, HCOs cannot use the federal companionship or live-in exemptions [S40].
- **Travel time** between clients during the workday is paid time [S39], and **mileage** for driving between clients and client errands must be reimbursed (Labor Code §2802) [S37]; the 2026 IRS rate is 72.5¢/mile [S38].
- **Paid sick leave**: at least 40 hours / 5 days per year [S36].
- **Payroll taxes**: employer FICA 7.65% [S34]; UI 3.4% (new employer) and ETT 0.1% on the first $7,000 per employee; employees pay SDI 1.3% [S33].

### Systems
Scheduling, caregiver timekeeping and billing software; a training log; personnel files with registry, Live Scan and TB documentation. Medi-Cal-funded personal care requires EVV [S43].

sections.financial_narrative:
### How the model is built
Capacity is the active client census the office is sized for; occupancy (90% default) is the share actually on service in a month (operator assumption). Revenue = hourly rate × billable hours.
- **Private pay:** $40/hour (CareScout California median) [S24] × **80 billable hours per client-month** (about 18.5 hours a week — operator estimate, verify locally).
- **Medi-Cal PCHS:** $33/hour, the DHCS non-binding midpoint [S19] — an **assumption**, since plans negotiate rates — × 60 authorized hours per member-month (operator estimate).
- **Caregivers:** $20.40/hour (San Diego County IHSS wage [S21]) for billable hours plus 5% paid non-billable time (travel between clients [S39], training [S14]; operator estimate).
- **Office staff:** San Diego metro BLS medians — administrator $79,770 [S27], supervisor $49,570 [S26], scheduler $51,650 [S28]. The 20-client owner-operator takes $55,490 (10th percentile) [S27].
- **Payroll burden 19.5%:** 9.5% taxes (FICA, UI, ETT, FUTA) [S34][S33], 6% workers' comp (operator estimate; mandatory coverage [S4]), 4% benefits incl. paid sick leave [S36].
- **Required fixed costs:** HCO renewal $5,603 ÷ 24 [S2]; $800 LLC tax and the gross-receipts LLC fee ($2,500–$6,000 by size) [S41]; liability insurance and bond at the required minimums [S4] (premiums are estimates). Office rent at $2.75/sq ft/month is an operator estimate.
- **Per-client costs:** caregiver mileage (40 miles × 72.5¢) [S37][S38], HCA registration/Live Scan/TB for replacement hires [S15], software, insurance exposure, recruiting, supplies, 1.5% card/ACH fees (estimates).

### Results at 90% census
| Configuration | Monthly net | Margin | Break-even census |
|---|---|---|---|
| Private pay, 75 clients | +$27,386 | 12.7% | 39.5 clients (53%) |
| Mixed 60 clients (70% private / 30% PCHS) | +$15,405 | 10.1% | 34.2 clients (57%) |
| Private pay, 40 clients (default) | +$9,057 | 7.9% | 26.7 clients (67%) |
| Private pay, 20 clients (owner-administrator) | +$3,909 | 6.8% | 14.0 clients (70%) |
| PCHS only, 100 members | −$9,032 | −5.1% | not reached (≈118 members) |

At 80% census the private 40 agency nets +$5,148 and the 20-client agency +$1,955.

### Unit economics
One private-pay client brings $3,200 a month (80 h × $40). The caregiver costs 84 paid hours × $20.40 × 1.195 ≈ $2,048, and per-client expenses about $175, leaving **≈ $977 per client per month** for the office. A PCHS member brings $1,980 (60 h × $33) and leaves only **≈ $317** after the same costs, so a PCHS-only agency cannot cover a full office. **The 100-member PCHS agency breaks even at about $34.67/hour** (it nets +$1,768 at $35, +$17,968 at the $38 high, and −$30,632 at the $29 low). In the mixed agency, PCHS at $29 cuts the result to +$11,517; at $38 it rises to +$20,265.

### Sensitivity (operator estimates — verify locally)
- **60 billable hours per client instead of 80:** private 40 −$1,313; private 20 −$1,276; private 75 +$7,942; mixed 60 +$4,516. The 40-client agency breaks even at about 62–63 hours per client-month.
- **Price $36 instead of $40:** private 40 −$2,463; private 20 −$1,851; private 75 +$5,786. Break-even price ≈ $36.86 for the 40-client agency and ≈ $37.29 for the 20-client agency.
- **Price $44:** private 40 +$20,577.
- **Caregiver wage $22.00 instead of $20.40:** private 40 +$3,275; private 20 +$1,019; private 75 +$16,545; mixed 60 +$7,382; PCHS 100 −$19,873.
- **Lower-wage market:** the model wage is above every 2026 local minimum found (highest Emeryville $20.34 [S30]); paying the unincorporated LA County minimum of $18.47 is legal [S30] but below the LA County IHSS wage ($19.64 [S21]) and would make hiring harder.

The private-pay result is most sensitive to hours sold per client and to the spread between price and caregiver wage.
sections.risks:
- **Caregiver wage competition.** IHSS pays $19.64–$23.00 in the largest counties [S21] and lets family members be paid, so agencies must match or beat it. Each $1.60/hour wage increase costs the 40-client agency about $5,800 a month (see Section 8).
- **Price and hours risk.** At $36/hour or 60 hours per client the 40-client private agency loses money; hold minimum visit lengths and price to local competitors.
- **No published Medi-Cal rate.** PCHS rates are negotiated with each plan; DHCS's benchmark is non-binding and built on a $15 wage [S19]. A PCHS-only agency needs about $34.67/hour to break even.
- **PCHS is secondary to IHSS.** Plans must keep IHSS primary and cannot use PCHS in place of an IHSS referral; HCBA members receiving WPCS are ineligible [S17]. Authorizations can be short.
- **Licensing delays.** CDSS publishes no processing time and returns incomplete packets [S3]; you pay rent and insurance while waiting.
- **Unannounced inspections and enforcement.** CDSS may inspect without notice and can deny, suspend or revoke for violations, conduct inimical to clients, disqualifying convictions or financial malfeasance [S11][S12].
- **Employment-law exposure.** Unpaid travel time, unreimbursed mileage and overtime errors are common claims [S39][S37][S40]. Live-in and 24-hour arrangements need counsel (not verified here).
- **Insurance cost.** Required $1M/$3M liability, workers' comp and bond [S4]; home care workers' comp classes run above the $1.65 per $100 statewide average [S35] — get quotes before pricing.
- **Competition.** 2,247 licensed HCOs and 210 pending (May 2025) [S23].
- **New training rule.** Dementia training becomes mandatory in annual training from 1/1/2027 [S14].
- **ACA employer mandate at larger census.** At about 75 private-pay clients or 100 PCHS members (90% census), the agency reaches roughly 50 full-time-equivalent employees and becomes an ACA applicable large employer [S48]. It must then offer affordable health coverage to full-time (30+ h/week) staff or face IRC 4980H penalties. The model's 4% benefits load does not cover this; get a quote, or keep most aides under 30 hours a week. The 40-client private agency (~28 FTE) and the 60-client mixed agency (~38 FTE) are below the threshold.
sections.recommendations:
1. **Lead with private pay.** Price at or above the $40 California median [S24] after checking local competitors; the 40-client agency breaks even near $36.86/hour.
2. **Sell hours, not visits.** Set minimum visit lengths (e.g., 4 hours) and target 80+ billable hours per client-month; at 60 hours the 40-client agency loses money.
3. **Pay to win caregivers.** Budget at least your county's IHSS wage ($20.40 San Diego, $19.64 Los Angeles [S21]) and pay travel time and mileage [S39][S37]; price so the spread over wage stays near $19–20/hour.
4. **Start lean, then scale.** Begin as an owner-operator (20 clients, +$3,900/month) and add a supervisor and scheduler as you pass ~30 clients; at 75 clients the margin reaches 12.7%.
5. **Add Medi-Cal PCHS selectively.** Contract with plans for PCHS/Respite only at rates near or above $35/hour and with authorized hours that fit your scheduling; keep it a minority of revenue (the 70/30 mix nets +$15,400 at $33) [S17][S19].
6. **File a complete packet once.** Bind insurance, the $10,000 bond and HCS 402 before mailing; name a designee other than the licensee on HCS 308; include the training plan and policies [S3][S4].
7. **Build compliance into hiring.** Registry clearance, Live Scan, TB and 5 hours of training before any client contact; notify CDSS when aides leave; add dementia content to annual training before January 2027 [S6][S7][S14].
8. **Develop referral sources** — discharge planners, senior living, care managers, elder-law attorneys and plan care managers — and track cost per client acquired.
9. **Keep a cash reserve** for the ramp: the model's 40-client agency runs a cumulative deficit of about $125,000 before turning profitable in month 11.

corrections_vs_previous: Old checklist cited 'HSC 1796.37(g)' for the $10,000 employee dishonesty bond. The bond requirement is in HSC §1796.37 (licensure) and §1796.42(c) (ongoing operation); there is no subdivision (g) for it [S4][S5].

Old checklist cited 'HSC 1796.30, 1796.48' for Live Scan background checks. Background check requirements are in HSC §1796.23–§1796.28 as applied by §1796.43, and the licensee background exam is required by §1796.37 (background exam under §1796.33) [S6][S4].

Old checklist cited 'HSC 1796.63' for a post-licensure inspection and told owners to 'schedule' it. CDSS conducts random, unannounced inspections under HSC §1796.52 and may enter during business hours without notice (§1796.53) [S49]; there is no scheduled pre- or post-licensure inspection to request [S11].

Old checklist described the 5-hour entry-level training as '2 hours orientation, 3 hours core competencies'. The statute requires 2 hours of orientation and 3 hours of safety training before client contact, plus 5 hours annually; SB 412 (Stats. 2025, ch. 414) adds dementia care to annual training from January 1, 2027 — the old file missed this change [S14].

Old checklist cited HSC §1796.44 (training) for aide Live Scan and HCA registration. Registry clearance, background checks and TB clearance before client contact are in §1796.43 and §1796.45 [S6][S7].

Old checklist omitted the TB examination (90 days before or within 7 days after hire, repeated every 2 years), the CDSS orientation the licensee must complete, the rule that the licensee cannot name him- or herself as designee on HCS 308, and the requirement to notify CDSS immediately when an aide leaves [S7][S4][S3][S6].

Old checklist stated as fact that 'failure to respond in 30 days may void your application' and gave a '3–12 weeks' processing estimate. Neither appears in CDSS materials reviewed; HCS 281 says incomplete packets are returned and review starts only on a complete packet with fee [S3].

Old checklist said dementia care is 'not permitted under HCO license'. The Act defines home care services broadly (non-medical help for people who cannot perform tasks because of age or disability) and from 2027 requires dementia training for aides — serving clients with dementia is within scope; medical/skilled care is not [S8][S14].

Old files contained no funding analysis. They did not explain that IHSS — California's largest home care program (930,755 recipients, Aug. 2026) — pays consumer-hired individual providers, not agencies (contract mode only in San Francisco), or that Medi-Cal money reaches HCOs mainly through managed care Community Supports contracts with no published rate [S21][S22][S17][S19].
